topics.title: STP: the big picture of segmentation
topics.summary: Marketers rarely try to sell to everyone. A customer-driven strategy has four steps: segmentation divides the market into groups, targeting chooses which groups to serve, differentiation makes the offering different and better, and positioning places it in target customers' minds. This topic defines segmentation, segments, target markets and product differentiation, and explains why firms segment at all.

topics.title: How narrowly to target, and whether a segment is worth it
topics.summary: Firms can target broadly or narrowly, from mass marketing to niche and one-to-one marketing. Segmenting only makes sense when it adds more revenue than cost. Two separate checklists help: five criteria for whether a segment is properly FORMED, and five criteria for which segments to SELECT as targets.

topics.title: Segmentation variables: consumer and business markets
topics.summary: Consumer markets are segmented with four families of variables: geographic (where), demographic (census facts), psychographic (personality, values, lifestyle) and behaviouristic (how people use the product, including usage rate and the 80/20 rule). Business markets add bases such as operating characteristics, purchasing approaches, situational factors and personal characteristics.

topics.title: From segments to targets: profiles, data, process and ethics
topics.summary: Marketers bring segments to life with target market profiles and personas, and buy data from firms such as Nielsen, Euromonitor and Environics Analytics. A six-step process moves from identifying needs to monitoring results, and a market-product grid shows where market size lies. Targeting also has to be socially responsible.

topics.title: Positioning the offering
topics.summary: Positioning is the place a brand holds in consumers' minds compared with competitors, built on image, product attributes and price. A firm can position head-to-head or look for a less-competitive niche (differentiation positioning), write the position down in a positioning statement, check it on a perceptual map, change it through repositioning, and build it on points-of-parity, points-of-difference and a USP.

concepts.definition: A customer-driven marketing strategy has two decisions: select customers to serve (segmentation: divide the total market into smaller segments; targeting: select the segment or segments to enter) and decide on a value proposition (differentiation: differentiate the market offering to create superior customer value; positioning: position the offering in the minds of target customers).
concepts.explain: Think of STP as a funnel from 'who could buy' to 'who we serve and how they see us'. First you slice the market into groups (segmentation), then pick the group(s) worth pursuing (targeting). Only then do you decide what will make your offering different (differentiation) and the place you want it to hold in those customers' minds (positioning). Everything aims at the centre of the model: create value for targeted customers.
concepts.example: A Calgary craft brewery splits beer drinkers into segments, targets young adults who like sour beers, makes the only sours brewed with locally foraged fruit (differentiation), and positions itself as 'Calgary's adventurous brewery'.
concepts.contrast: Segmentation = dividing the market; targeting = choosing which segment(s) to enter; differentiation = making the offering different and better; positioning = the place the offering holds in target customers' minds. Segmentation and targeting answer 'whom do we serve?'; differentiation and positioning answer 'with what value?'
concepts.trap: Watch the verbs: 'divide/group' = segmentation, 'select/choose/enter' = targeting, 'make different/superior value' = differentiation, 'in the minds of' = positioning. Stems often describe a firm that has ALREADY divided the market and is now choosing a group, which is targeting, not segmentation.
concepts.mnemonic: Slice, Select, Stand out, Settle in the mind (S-T-D-P).

concepts.definition: Aggregating prospective buyers into groups (segments) that (1) have common needs and (2) will respond similarly to a marketing action.
concepts.explain: Segmentation means grouping, not just splitting: you gather buyers who are alike in what they need and in how they react to marketing. The resulting groups are relatively homogeneous, with similar consumption behaviour, attitudes and target market profiles. Because each group wants something a bit different, segmentation leads to product differentiation.
concepts.example: A Winnipeg hockey retailer groups customers into hockey parents, adult rec-league players and elite juniors, because each group needs different gear and responds differently to promotions.
concepts.contrast: Segmentation groups the market; targeting chooses which group(s) to pursue. Segmentation is also the opposite of mass marketing, which treats the whole market as one group with one marketing mix.
concepts.trap: Both conditions are required: common needs AND a similar response to a marketing action. If the stem says the firm 'decided which group to pursue', that is targeting, not segmentation.
concepts.mnemonic: Same needs + same response = same segment.

concepts.definition: Market segments are the relatively homogeneous groups of prospective buyers that segmentation produces. A target market is the specific group of existing and potential consumers to which marketers direct their marketing efforts.
concepts.explain: Segmentation can produce many segments; the target market is the one (or few) the firm actually picks. Members of a segment are similar to each other in consumption behaviour, attitudes and profile, but they do not have to be identical. A target market includes both people who already buy and people the firm hopes will buy.
concepts.example: Fjord Kayak Co. identifies five segments of paddlers in Western Canada but directs all its ads at one of them: retired outdoor enthusiasts on Vancouver Island. That group is its target market.
concepts.contrast: A segment is any group identified in the market; a target market is the segment(s) chosen for marketing efforts. A persona is a character description of the typical customer in a target market, not the group itself.
concepts.trap: 'Existing AND potential': a target market is not just current customers. Also watch for options claiming segment members must be identical; they only need to be relatively homogeneous.
concepts.mnemonic: Many segments, one bullseye.

concepts.definition: A strategy that uses different marketing mix activities, such as product features and advertising, to help consumers perceive a product as different from and better than competing products.
concepts.explain: Once you know segments want different things, you can offer different versions of your product (or different messages) so each group sees your offering as the better choice for them. A firm selling two or more products with different features aimed at different segments is using product differentiation. It is the firm-side strategy that segmentation leads to.
concepts.example: Hallmark sells several card brands, such as Shoebox, Mahogany and Tree of Life, each designed for a different segment.
concepts.contrast: Product differentiation (offering distinct products or marketing so they are seen as different and better) is not differentiation positioning (placing ONE brand in a smaller, less-competitive niche by stressing unique attributes). It is also not behavioural or usage segmentation, which are ways of grouping buyers.
concepts.trap: Several brands or models from one firm, each aimed at a different segment = product differentiation. Don't be pulled toward 'behavioural segmentation' or 'usage segmentation'; those describe how buyers are grouped, not the strategy of offering distinct products.
concepts.mnemonic: Different features for different folks.

concepts.definition: Marketers segment because (1) consumers have a range of different needs, (2) companies have limited amounts of money, and (3) marketers need clear consumer insights on their target markets.
concepts.explain: One product rarely satisfies everyone, budgets can't reach everyone, and good decisions need a clear picture of who you serve. Segmenting focuses money on groups whose needs you understand and can meet. Movies made for different audiences are a classic illustration.
concepts.example: A Saskatoon bakery with an $8,000 annual budget spends it all reaching nearby office workers instead of advertising city-wide.
concepts.contrast: These are reasons TO segment. Don't mix them up with the five criteria for FORMING segments (e.g., similarity within, difference among) or the five criteria for SELECTING target segments (e.g., market size, expected growth).
concepts.trap: A distractor may present a forming criterion ('similarity of needs within a segment') or a selecting criterion ('market size') as a reason to segment. The three reasons are needs, money and insights.
concepts.mnemonic: Needs differ, Money is limited, Insight matters (N-M-I).

figure.title: Three reasons to segment
items: Consumers have a range of different needs
Companies have limited amounts of money
Marketers need clear consumer insights on their target markets

concepts.term: Target-market continuum: mass, segment, niche, individualized marketing
concepts.definition: Approaches to segmentation range from broad to narrow: mass (undifferentiated) marketing uses one product and one marketing mix for the entire market; segment (differentiated) marketing designs different offerings for different segments; niche marketing focuses on one or a few narrowly defined, specialized segments; individualized (one-to-one) marketing tailors offerings to individual customers, often through mass customization (tailoring goods or services to individual tastes on a high-volume scale).
concepts.explain: Picture a dial that runs from 'everyone' to 'just you'. Mass marketing treats the market as one big group. Segment marketing serves several groups with different offerings. Niche marketing zooms in on a small, specialized group. Individualized marketing treats each customer as a segment of one, and mass customization does this at high volume through build-to-order.
concepts.example: Table salt sold the same way to everyone (mass); a hotel company with budget, business and luxury brands (segment); racing bikes only for competitive cyclists over 50 (niche); sneakers built to each buyer's chosen design (mass customization).
concepts.contrast: Niche = one or a few narrow segments, which are still groups of people. Individualized marketing / mass customization = segments of one (each customer). Segment marketing serves several segments; mass marketing makes no distinction between segments.
concepts.trap: 'Build-to-order', 'each customer designs their own', 'high volume' = mass customization, not niche. 'Small, specialized group' = niche. 'One product, one mix, entire market' = mass. 'Differentiated marketing' is another name for segment marketing.
concepts.mnemonic: Mass > Segment > Niche > Individual (Many, Some, Few, One).

figure.title: Broad to narrow target-market continuum
items: Mass marketing (undifferentiated): one product and one marketing mix for the entire market
Segment marketing (differentiated): different offerings for different segments
Niche marketing: one or a few narrowly defined, specialized segments
Individualized (one-to-one) marketing / mass customization: tailored to individual customers on a high-volume scale

concepts.definition: A firm segments its market only when doing so increases sales revenue, profit and ROI; if the added expenses more than offset the added revenue, it should not segment further. The ways to segment are one product with multiple market segments, multiple products with multiple market segments, and segments of one (mass customization).
concepts.explain: Segmenting is a business decision, not an automatic good. One product for multiple segments (e.g., a TV show or magazine that several audiences enjoy) is cheap, because the main extra cost is promotion. Multiple products for multiple segments (different models for different groups) costs more but fits each segment better. Segments of one take this down to the individual customer. Stop when the extra cost outweighs the extra revenue.
concepts.example: A family TV drama that appeals to young children, teens and older adults is one product serving multiple segments; a carmaker selling a hatchback, a minivan and a luxury sedan to different groups is using multiple products for multiple segments.
concepts.contrast: One product/multiple segments = same product, different promotion (low cost). Multiple products/multiple segments = different products (higher cost, better fit). Segments of one = mass customization.
concepts.trap: If a stem says added expenses exceed added revenue, the answer is 'do not segment further', not layoffs, cutting quality or dropping products. A single TV show or magazine aimed at several groups is ONE product with multiple segments, not mass customization.
concepts.mnemonic: Keep segmenting only while revenue gained > cost added.

concepts.definition: Five criteria for forming market segments: (1) potential for increased profit and ROI; (2) similarity of needs of potential buyers within a segment; (3) difference of needs of buyers among segments; (4) feasibility of a marketing action to reach a segment; (5) simplicity and cost of assigning potential buyers to segments.
concepts.explain: These criteria test whether a proposed segment is worth creating at all. Buyers inside the segment should be alike, the segments should differ from each other, a marketing action must be able to reach the segment, it must be simple and cheap to tell who belongs, and the whole thing must pay off in profit and ROI.
concepts.example: A restaurant considering a separate salad bar for the 2-3% of people mildly allergic to preservatives fails 'potential for increased profit and ROI', because the segment is small and a duplicate salad bar is costly.
concepts.contrast: Forming criteria judge whether segments are well built (similar within, different among, reachable, easy to assign, profitable). SELECTING criteria (market size, expected growth, competitive position, cost of reaching, compatibility with objectives and resources) choose which of the formed segments to target.
concepts.trap: 'Difference AMONG' versus 'similarity WITHIN': reversed wording is a common distractor. 'Simplicity and cost of assigning' (can we tell who belongs?) is different from 'feasibility of a marketing action' (can we reach them?). Expected growth and market size belong on the SELECTING list.
concepts.mnemonic: PSDFS: Profit, Same within, Different among, Feasible to reach, Simple to assign.

figure.title: Five criteria for FORMING segments
items: Potential for increased profit and return on investment (ROI)
Similarity of needs of potential buyers within a segment
Difference of needs of buyers among segments
Feasibility of a marketing action to reach a segment
Simplicity and cost of assigning potential buyers to segments

concepts.definition: Five criteria for choosing which segments to target: market size, expected growth, competitive position, cost of reaching the segment, and compatibility with the organization's objectives and resources.
concepts.explain: After segments are formed, the firm compares them. A big, growing segment is attractive, but not if strong rivals dominate it, if reaching it is too expensive, or if serving it doesn't fit what the organization wants to do and is able to do.
concepts.example: A Regina software firm passes on a large, fast-growing craft-brewery segment because serving it would need hardware-installation skills the firm lacks and doesn't fit its mission.
concepts.contrast: Selecting criteria answer 'which segment should we target?'; forming criteria answer 'is this a properly formed segment?'. 'Cost of reaching the segment' (selecting) is not the same as 'simplicity and cost of assigning buyers to segments' (forming).
concepts.trap: Distractors slip forming criteria (similarity within, difference among, feasibility, assigning) into a selecting question, and the reverse. The word 'cost' appears on both lists, so check whether it is the cost of REACHING (selecting) or of ASSIGNING (forming).
concepts.mnemonic: Size, Growth, Competition, Cost, Compatibility (SGC-CC).

figure.title: Five criteria for SELECTING target segments
items: Market size
Expected growth
Competitive position
Cost of reaching the segment
Compatibility with the organization's objectives and resources

concepts.definition: Consumer markets are segmented using four families of variables: geographic (where does the target market live and work?), demographic (what is its basic census-type information?), psychographic (what attitudes, values, interests, habits and approaches to life does it share?) and behaviouristic (how does it use and interact with the product?).
concepts.explain: Each family answers a different question about the customer. Real segments usually combine families, for example a region (geographic) plus a music preference (psychographic). Classify each piece of a description separately.
concepts.example: 'Women aged 25-34 (demographic) in suburban Calgary (geographic) who value sustainability (psychographic) and use a reusable cup five times a week (behaviouristic).'
concepts.contrast: Demographic = statistical facts about who people are; psychographic = their inner life (personality, values, lifestyle, interests); behaviouristic = their relationship with the product (usage, benefits sought, loyalty, occasion); geographic = location and climate. Business markets add other bases, such as operating characteristics.
concepts.trap: Stems often hide two families in one scenario (East vs West = geographic; liking country music = psychographic). Interests and music taste are psychographic, NOT demographic.
concepts.mnemonic: Where, Who on paper, Who inside, How they use (G-D-P-B).

figure.title: Segmentation variables in consumer markets

Guiding question
Example variables
rows: Where does the target market live and work?
What is the basic census-type information on the target market as a whole?
Age, gender, income, education, occupation, ethnicity, family life cycle, household size, generation

concepts.definition: Segmenting by where the target market lives and works, using variables such as region, city size, urban/suburban/rural location and climate.
concepts.explain: Location shapes needs: winter climate drives snowblower sales, and tastes can differ between regions. Geographic variables help decide where to sell and where to concentrate distribution and advertising.
concepts.example: A hardware chain stocks more block heaters and snowblowers in Thunder Bay than in Victoria, BC, because of the climate.
concepts.contrast: Geographic is about place (region, city size, climate). It is not demographic (age, income), even though census data often reports both together.
concepts.trap: 'Eastern vs Western Canada', 'urban vs rural', 'cold climates' = geographic. If the stem also mentions tastes or interests, the answer is often a two-family combination.
concepts.mnemonic: Geo = where on the globe.

concepts.definition: Segmenting by basic census-type information about the target market: age, gender, income, education, occupation, ethnicity, family life cycle, household size and generation.
concepts.explain: Demographics are the easy-to-measure statistical facts about who customers are. They are widely available and often the starting point, but people with identical demographics can still differ greatly in values and behaviour.
concepts.example: A daycare-supply company targets households with children under five and incomes over $90,000.
concepts.contrast: Demographic = who you are on paper (age, income, life stage). Psychographic = who you are inside (personality, values, lifestyle). 'Generation' (e.g., Gen Z) is demographic; 'adventurous' is psychographic.
concepts.trap: Lifestyle and interests are NOT demographic. Family life cycle and household size ARE demographic, even though they sound like lifestyle.
concepts.mnemonic: Demographic = data from a census form.

concepts.definition: Segmenting by the prevailing attitudes, values, interests, habits and approaches to life a target market shares, including lifestyle (activities, interests and opinions, or AIO), personality and values.
concepts.explain: Psychographics capture the 'why' inside the customer. Two people of the same age and income may buy very differently because one is a thrill-seeker and the other a careful planner. Music preference, a collector's personality and personal values all count as psychographic.
concepts.example: Nike targets 'keepers': people who buy Air Jordans, keep them under the bed and show them off to friends. That is a personality/lifestyle segment.
concepts.contrast: Psychographic (personality, values, lifestyle, interests) vs behaviouristic (how people use the product: usage rate, benefits sought, loyalty, occasion, user status) vs demographic (age, income, gender).
concepts.trap: 'Keepers', 'collectors', 'adventurous', 'country-music fans', 'value sustainability' = psychographic. Don't pick 'behaviour' or 'usage' just because the stem describes something people do; ask whether it reflects personality and lifestyle or how the product is used.
concepts.mnemonic: Psycho-graphic = a graph of the psyche (AIO + personality + values).

concepts.definition: Segmenting by how the target market uses and interacts with the product: product features or benefits sought, usage rate, user status, loyalty status and purchase occasion.
concepts.explain: Behaviouristic variables look at the customer's relationship with the product itself: what benefit they want from it, how much they use it, whether they are a non-user, first-time user or ex-user, how loyal they are, and when or why they buy.
concepts.example: A toothpaste brand offers whitening, cavity-protection and sensitivity versions, which is segmentation by benefits sought.
concepts.contrast: Behaviouristic = product use and interaction. Psychographic = personality, values and lifestyle in general. 'Buys only our brand' (loyalty status) is behaviouristic, even though it sounds like an attitude.
concepts.trap: Benefits sought, user status, loyalty, occasion and usage rate are all behaviouristic. 'Ex-user / first-time user' is user status, not loyalty. 'Valentine's Day buyers' is purchase occasion.
concepts.mnemonic: B-U-U-L-O: Benefits sought, Usage rate, User status, Loyalty status, Occasion.

concepts.definition: Usage rate is the quantity consumed or patronage (store visits) during a specific period. The 80/20 rule is a concept that suggests 80 percent of a firm's sales are obtained from 20 percent of its customers.
concepts.explain: Usage rate sorts customers into heavy, medium, light and non-users. Because a small group of heavy users often produces most of the sales, firms protect and reward them, which is why frequency and loyalty programs exist.
concepts.example: If a pizzeria's sales follow the 80/20 rule, its top 400 of 2,000 customers produce $400,000 of its $500,000 in sales.
concepts.contrast: Usage rate (how much or how often) differs from loyalty status (how committed a buyer is to one brand). The 80/20 rule links a share of CUSTOMERS (20%) to a share of SALES (80%).
concepts.trap: Watch for flipped numbers: '80% of sales from 80% of customers' is wrong, while 'the other 80% of customers produce about 20% of sales' is simply the complement and is consistent with the rule. Usage rate is behaviouristic, not demographic or psychographic.
concepts.mnemonic: A few heavy users carry the load: 20 percent of people, 80 percent of sales.

concepts.definition: Business markets can be segmented by demographics (NAICS industry code, number of employees, sales, location) plus additional bases: operating characteristics (technology, user status, capabilities), purchasing approaches (centralized vs decentralized buying, buying criteria, relationships), situational factors (urgency, order size, specific application) and personal characteristics (buyer-seller similarity, attitude toward risk, loyalty).
concepts.explain: Organizations buy differently from consumers, so B2B marketers add bases that describe how a company operates and buys. These help match sales approaches, service levels and products to each type of business customer.
concepts.example: A Calgary pipe-fitting distributor offers premium rush delivery to oil-field clients who need emergency parts. That is segmentation by situational factors (urgency, order size).
concepts.contrast: Operating characteristics = what the company uses and can do; purchasing approaches = how it buys; situational factors = the circumstances of the order; personal characteristics = traits of the individual buyers (risk attitude, similarity, loyalty). Lifestyle (AIO) is a consumer psychographic variable, not a B2B base.
concepts.trap: Urgency and order size = situational factors, not purchasing approaches. Centralized vs decentralized buying = purchasing approaches. User status sits under operating characteristics in B2B, but is behaviouristic in consumer markets.
concepts.mnemonic: D-O-P-S-P: Demographics, Operating, Purchasing, Situational, Personal.

Example variables

Centralized vs decentralized buying, buying criteria, buyer-seller relationships
Buyer-seller similarity, attitude toward risk, loyalty

concepts.definition: A target market profile is a detailed description of the typical customer (demographics, psychographics, media habits and needs). Personas are character descriptions of a brand's typical customer, often with a name, photo and back-story.
concepts.explain: Personas turn segment data into a believable person, so everyone on the team designs products, messages and media plans for 'someone' real. A persona might be 'Kayla, the Planner', complete with her age, job, goals, worries and favourite apps.
concepts.example: Bow River Bank's persona 'Kayla, the Planner': 29, works in HR in Calgary, saving for a condo, reads personal-finance blogs, values security.
concepts.contrast: A segment is a GROUP of buyers; a persona is a single fictional CHARACTER representing its typical member. A perceptual map plots brands, not customers.
concepts.trap: A named, photographed, story-like description of one 'typical customer' = persona. A persona doesn't replace segmentation; it is built from it.
concepts.mnemonic: Persona = a person standing in for the segment.

concepts.definition: Research companies such as Nielsen or Euromonitor provide general consumer and lifestyle trend data, while companies such as Environics Analytics (PRIZM) provide more granular data that pinpoints population clusters (e.g., 'Middle-Class Mosaic').
concepts.explain: Marketers buy data to build segments. Broad trend reports show where the overall market is heading; cluster systems like PRIZM sort neighbourhoods into named lifestyle groups down to small geographic areas, which helps with store locations and local targeting.
concepts.example: A Toronto retailer checks which PRIZM clusters live within 5 km of a proposed store before signing a lease.
concepts.contrast: Nielsen / Euromonitor = general, broad consumer and lifestyle trends. Environics Analytics / PRIZM = granular, pinpointed population clusters.
concepts.trap: 'Granular', 'population clusters', 'neighbourhood', or named clusters like 'Middle-Class Mosaic' point to Environics/PRIZM. 'General trends' points to Nielsen or Euromonitor.
concepts.mnemonic: Environics = Exact neighbourhoods; Nielsen/Euromonitor = the big picture.

concepts.term: Six-step process for segmenting a market
concepts.definition: (1) Identify consumer/customer needs and common characteristics in the market; (2) cluster common consumer/customer variables to create meaningful market segments; (3) estimate the size and feasibility of each segment; (4) identify the segment(s) to be targeted; (5) take actions with marketing programs to reach the segment(s); (6) monitor and evaluate the success of these programs compared with objectives.
concepts.explain: The steps move from understanding (needs) to grouping (clusters) to sizing (how big and how realistic) to choosing (targets) to doing (marketing programs) to checking (results against objectives). Each step needs the output of the one before it.
concepts.example: A Kelowna winery identifies buyers' needs, groups them into four segments, sizes each with census and sales data, picks two to target, launches campaigns, then compares results with its sales objectives.
concepts.contrast: Estimating size and feasibility (step 3) comes BEFORE choosing targets (step 4). Taking action (step 5) comes before monitoring (step 6). Clustering (step 2) is the segmentation step; step 4 is targeting.
concepts.trap: Watch 'immediately after' questions: after clustering comes estimating size and feasibility, not targeting. 'Compared with objectives' always signals step 6.
concepts.mnemonic: I Can Estimate If Teams Measure (Identify, Cluster, Estimate, Identify targets, Take action, Monitor).

figure.title: Six-step process for segmenting a market
items: 1. Identify consumer/customer needs and common characteristics in the market
2. Cluster common consumer/customer variables to create meaningful market segments
3. Estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
4. Identify the segment(s) to be targeted
5. Take actions with marketing programs to reach the segment(s)
6. Monitor and evaluate the success of these programs compared with objectives

concepts.definition: A framework relating the market segments of potential buyers (rows) to the products offered or potential marketing actions (columns); each cell shows the estimated size of the market.
concepts.explain: The grid shows at a glance which product-segment combinations are big enough to pursue. Large cells suggest where to focus; small or empty cells suggest where not to.
concepts.example: Polar Bikes lists commuters, mountain riders and kids as rows and its bike models as columns, writing the estimated market size in each cell.
concepts.contrast: Market-product grid = segments x products, with market-size estimates. Perceptual map = brands plotted by consumer perception on two attributes. Persona = a description of one typical customer.
concepts.trap: Rows and columns of segments and products, or 'estimated market size in each cell', means a market-product grid. Two perceptual dimensions means a perceptual map.
concepts.mnemonic: Grid = Segments down, Products across, Size inside.

concepts.definition: Segmentation and targeting raise legal and ethical issues: marketers must avoid consumer backlash and take special care with vulnerable groups, disadvantaged groups and potentially harmful products. Social responsibility can be more important than profits if marketing is viewed as exploitative or irresponsible.
concepts.explain: A profitable segment is not automatically one you should target. Aiming risky products at children, or high-cost offers at people in financial hardship, can cause harm, public outrage and long-term damage to the brand.
concepts.example: An energy-drink brand decides not to target 13- to 15-year-olds even though that segment is growing fast.
concepts.contrast: An ethical screen asks 'SHOULD we target this group?'; the selecting criteria ask 'is this group ATTRACTIVE?'. A segment can pass the size and growth criteria and still be inappropriate to target.
concepts.trap: Know all four slide items: consumer backlash, vulnerable groups (e.g., children), disadvantaged groups (e.g., low-income people) and potentially harmful products. The course says responsibility can outweigh profits when marketing looks exploitative.
concepts.mnemonic: Back-off list: Backlash, Vulnerable, Disadvantaged, Harmful.

concepts.definition: The impression of the branded product a marketer wants to establish in consumers' minds relative to their needs and in contrast to the competition; that is, the place a product occupies in consumers' minds on important attributes relative to competitive products.
concepts.explain: Positioning happens in the customer's head; the marketer's job is to shape it. It rests on three basic factors (image, product attributes and price), and every element of the marketing mix must support it. Once established, the position must be maintained through consistent performance and communication.
concepts.example: Chiquita put its brand on bananas, a commodity, and promoted them as consistently high-quality fruit, giving the brand a distinct place in shoppers' minds.
concepts.contrast: Positioning (the place in consumers' minds) vs product differentiation (using features and advertising to make products seem different and better) vs repositioning (changing a position that already exists).
concepts.trap: A mix decision that contradicts the position (a premium brand sold in discount bins) is a positioning failure. Market size and expected growth are targeting criteria, not positioning factors.
concepts.mnemonic: IAP: Image, Attributes, Price, with every mix arrow pointing the same way.

figure.title: Keys to successful positioning
items: All marketing mix efforts must support the positioning strategy
Maintain the position through consistent performance and communication
Build on three basic factors: image, product attributes, price

concepts.definition: Head-to-head positioning means competing directly with competitors on similar product attributes in the same target market. Differentiation positioning means seeking a less-competitive, smaller market niche in which to locate a brand by stressing its unique attributes.
concepts.explain: Head-to-head is a direct fight: same customers, same attributes, 'we're better, faster or cheaper'. Differentiation positioning steps away from the crowd: find a small niche where your unique features matter and big rivals aren't fighting.
concepts.example: Children's Advil claiming it works faster and longer than Children's Tylenol (head-to-head); BMW's $495 Streetcarver skateboard with unique car-inspired stabilizers (differentiation positioning).
concepts.contrast: Head-to-head = same market, similar attributes, direct comparison. Differentiation positioning = smaller, less-competitive niche, unique attributes. Product differentiation (several distinct products for different segments) is a different idea.
concepts.trap: Comparison claims against a named rival on the same attribute = head-to-head. 'The only one with...' plus a small premium niche = differentiation positioning. Options like 'lateral', 'cognitive', 'distinction' or 'parallel market' positioning are not course terms.
concepts.mnemonic: Head-to-head = nose to nose; differentiation = find your own corner.

concepts.definition: A formalized statement that identifies the image a branded product represents in the market and what sets it apart from the competition. Template: 'For (target market) who desire (target market need), (brand) is the (product category) that offers (product benefits).'
concepts.explain: The statement is an internal guide that keeps everyone aligned on whom the brand serves, what need it meets, what category it competes in and which benefits set it apart. It is usually not the ad slogan itself.
concepts.example: For busy Calgary parents who desire healthy dinners in 15 minutes, FreshFork is the meal-kit service that offers pre-chopped, dietitian-approved ingredients.
concepts.contrast: Positioning statement = a full sentence with target, need, brand, category and benefits. USP = the single competitive advantage the positioning may rest on. Slogan = a short consumer-facing line.
concepts.trap: Know the template's five slots in order: target market, need ('who desire'), brand, product category, product benefits. If the 'who desire' clause is missing, the need is missing.
concepts.mnemonic: For WHO, who WANT what, BRAND is the CATEGORY that GIVES benefits.

concepts.definition: A means of displaying or graphing, in two dimensions, the location of products or brands in the minds of consumers.
concepts.explain: Researchers ask consumers how they see competing brands on two important attributes (e.g., price and luxury) and plot the results. The map shows which brands compete most closely, where gaps exist and where a brand might move. Comparative claims only work against brands consumers already see as worse on the chosen attribute.
concepts.example: On a drinks map with 'nutritious' on the vertical axis, coffee sits above sugared soft drinks but below skinny lattes and fruit-flavoured drinks, so a 'healthier than' coffee ad should compare coffee only with sugared soft drinks.
concepts.contrast: Perceptual map = the tool that shows perceived positions. Repositioning = the strategy of changing a brand's place (a move on the map). Market-product grid = segments x products with market sizes.
concepts.trap: On comparison questions, pick only the brands positioned LOWER than yours on the relevant axis. Two dimensions + consumer perceptions = perceptual map, not market-product grid.
concepts.mnemonic: Map the mind on two lines.

concepts.definition: Changing the place a product occupies in consumers' minds relative to competitive products, to more accurately meet consumer needs.
concepts.explain: Repositioning is for products that already have a position that no longer works: the image is dated, the use is too narrow, or needs have shifted. The brand gives consumers new reasons, uses or associations, moving its dot on the perceptual map.
concepts.example: Post Grape-Nuts, seen as 'something grandfather ate', promoted the cereal as a crunchy topping for yogurt, salad and soup, expanding its use from breakfast to all day.
concepts.contrast: Positioning creates the initial place; repositioning changes an existing one. A perceptual map is the tool that can show the move, not the strategy itself.
concepts.trap: Declining share + dated image + new uses or a new audience = repositioning, not 'product positioning' or 'perceptual mapping'. A brand-new product's first image is positioning.
concepts.mnemonic: RE-position = position AGAIN.

concepts.definition: Points-of-parity (POPs) are attribute or benefit associations that are not necessarily unique to the brand but may be shared with other brands. Points-of-difference (PODs) are attributes or benefits consumers strongly associate with a brand, positively evaluate, and believe they could not find to the same extent with a competitive brand.
concepts.explain: POPs are the basics a brand needs in order to be considered in its category: its 'ticket to play'. PODs are why customers choose it over rivals: its 'reason to win'. A POD must pass all three tests: strong association, positive evaluation, and not available to the same extent elsewhere.
concepts.example: The course uses Sobeys to illustrate POPs (features shared with other grocers) and Tim Hortons to illustrate PODs (associations Canadians feel no rival matches).
concepts.contrast: POP = shared and expected (ticket to play). POD = unique, valued and hard to match (reason to win). A well-liked attribute that every competitor also offers is still a POP.
concepts.trap: 'Shared with other brands' = POP, even if customers love it. 'Could not find to the same extent with a competitor' = POD. A USP is a single strong POD used as the basis for positioning.
concepts.mnemonic: Parity = par for the course; Difference = distinctive.

concepts.definition: When choosing a competitive advantage on which to base positioning, a firm can build on one unique selling proposition (USP), a single distinctive benefit that sets the brand apart, or on multiple differences.
concepts.explain: A USP is the one clear reason to buy that the brand repeats everywhere. It should be something customers value and competitors can't easily match; in effect, a single strong point-of-difference. Some brands instead position on several differences at once.
concepts.example: Swift Pizza's only message, on every ad and box: 'Hot at your door in 20 minutes or it's free.'
concepts.contrast: USP = one distinctive advantage. Multiple-differences positioning = several advantages. Positioning statement = the full template sentence. POP = a shared attribute, which makes a poor USP.
concepts.trap: An attribute every competitor offers equally well can't be a USP (it's a POP). 'One single reason or benefit, promoted consistently' = USP.
concepts.mnemonic: USP = Unique, Single, Promoted.

activities.title: Order the six segmentation steps
activities.prompt: Put the six steps for segmenting a market in the correct order.
items: Identify consumer/customer needs and common characteristics in the market
Cluster common consumer/customer variables to create meaningful market segments
Estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
Identify the segment(s) to be targeted
Take actions with marketing programs to reach the segment(s)
Monitor and evaluate the success of these programs compared with objectives
activities.explanation: You must understand needs before you can cluster buyers, and size the clusters before you can sensibly pick targets. Only after choosing targets can you build marketing programs, and you can only evaluate those programs against objectives after they run.

activities.title: Sort the segmentation variables
activities.prompt: Drag each variable into the consumer segmentation family it belongs to.
activities.explanation: Geographic = where people live and work; demographic = census-type facts such as income, life stage and generation; psychographic = personality, values and lifestyle (AIO); behaviouristic = how people use and interact with the product (usage rate, benefits sought, occasion, loyalty, user status).

activities.title: Match the positioning terms
activities.prompt: Match each positioning term with its best example or description.

pairs.right: Children's Advil claims it works faster and longer than Children's Tylenol
BMW Streetcarver: the only skateboard with car-inspired stabilizers, sold to a small premium niche
Grape-Nuts promoted as a topping for yogurt, salad and soup
A two-dimensional graph of where brands sit in consumers' minds
An attribute shared with competing brands, such as a grocer's loyalty card
An attribute consumers strongly link to the brand, value, and can't find to the same extent elsewhere
One single distinctive advantage the positioning is built on
For (target market) who desire (need), (brand) is the (category) that offers (benefits)

activities.explanation: Head-to-head attacks rivals on the same attributes in the same market, while differentiation positioning moves to a less-competitive niche. Repositioning changes an existing position, and a perceptual map is the tool that displays positions. POPs are shared, PODs are unique and valued, a USP is one chosen advantage, and the positioning statement puts the whole position into one formal sentence.

activities.title: Forming vs selecting criteria
activities.prompt: Is each item a criterion for FORMING segments or for SELECTING target segments?

items.text: Potential for increased profit and ROI
Similarity of needs of potential buyers within a segment
Difference of needs of buyers among segments
Feasibility of a marketing action to reach a segment
Simplicity and cost of assigning potential buyers to segments
Compatibility with the organization's objectives and resources

activities.explanation: Forming criteria check whether a segment is properly built: profitable, similar within, different among, reachable by a marketing action, and easy and cheap to assign buyers to. Selecting criteria compare formed segments to choose targets: size, growth, competition, cost of reaching, and fit with objectives and resources. Note the two different 'cost' items: assigning (forming) vs reaching (selecting).

activities.title: Broad to narrow targeting
activities.prompt: Order these approaches from the broadest target market to the narrowest.
items: Mass marketing
Segment marketing
Niche marketing
Individualized (one-to-one) marketing
activities.explanation: Mass marketing treats the whole market as one group; segment marketing serves several segments with different offerings; niche marketing focuses on one or a few narrow, specialized segments; individualized marketing (often mass customization) tailors offerings to each customer, a segment of one.

activities.title: Match the B2B segmentation bases
activities.prompt: Match each business-market segmentation base with its example variables.

pairs.right: NAICS industry code, number of employees, location
Centralized vs decentralized buying, buying criteria
Buyer-seller similarity, attitude toward risk, loyalty

activities.explanation: Business demographics describe the firm itself; operating characteristics describe what it uses and can do; purchasing approaches describe how it buys; situational factors describe the circumstances of an order; personal characteristics describe the individual buyers.
